treatments.name: Fluid and salt
treatments.does: Raises blood volume, so less of it pools in your legs when you stand.
treatments.detail: Up to 2–3 litres of water and 10–12 g of salt a day "may be considered".
treatments.evidence: Class IIb, Level E — the consensus panel’s weakest grade: expert opinion, not trial evidence.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Compression — above the waist of your socks
treatments.does: Stops blood pooling in the abdomen, which is where most of it goes.
treatments.detail: On a tilt table, heart rate fell step by step with how much of the body was compressed: 109 bpm with none, 103 with the lower legs, 97 with the abdomen and thighs, 92 with both.
treatments.evidence: Randomised crossover trial, 30 patients. Small, but it is a real trial with a dose-response.

treatments.name: Exercise, starting lying down
treatments.does: Rebuilds blood volume and heart size, which standing all day does not.
treatments.detail: A structured, graduated programme beginning with non-upright exercise — rowing machines, recumbent bikes, swimming — before anything upright.
treatments.evidence: Class IIa, Level B-R — "can be effective", supported by randomised data.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Reviewing the drugs you already take
treatments.does: Several common medications make orthostatic symptoms worse.
treatments.detail: Withdrawing medications that aggravate POTS is listed first among the non-drug measures.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Ivabradine
treatments.does: Slows the heart without lowering blood pressure.
treatments.detail: Standing heart rate fell from 94.2 to 77.9 bpm against placebo, with improved physical and social functioning.
treatments.evidence: The one randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a drug in POTS. 22 patients, hyperadrenergic subtype.

treatments.name: Beta-blockers (low-dose propranolol)
treatments.detail: Covered by the consensus statement as an option; doses are low, and higher doses can make fatigue worse.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Midodrine
treatments.does: Tightens blood vessels so less blood pools.
treatments.detail: Short-acting, taken before being upright; not at bedtime.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Fludrocortisone
treatments.does: Helps the body hold on to salt and water.
treatments.detail: Used alongside the salt and fluid measures rather than instead of them.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

treatments.name: Pyridostigmine
treatments.does: Acts on the autonomic signalling itself.
treatments.detail: Sometimes chosen when the gut symptoms are prominent.
treatments.source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

exercise_registry.headline: 71% of the people who finished no longer met the criteria for POTS.
exercise_registry.caveat: 103 of the 251 who enrolled finished. Counted against everyone who started, it is 29%.
exercise_registry.detail: Three months, 3–5 sessions a week, progressing from semi-recumbent to upright, with strength work and extra salt and fluid.

criteria.line: A sustained heart-rate rise of 30 bpm or more within 10 minutes of standing — 40 bpm if you are 12 to 19 — without a drop in blood pressure, with symptoms lasting at least three months.

no_approved_drug: No medication is approved by the FDA for POTS. Everything prescribed for it is prescribed off-label — which is legal, ordinary, and worth knowing before a pharmacist mentions it first.

not_anxiety.claim: People with POTS do not have more anxiety disorders than anyone else.
not_anxiety.body: Assessed formally against DSM-IV criteria, people with POTS showed no increased lifetime prevalence of anxiety disorders, panic disorder or major depression. They may look anxious — a racing heart on standing looks exactly like fear — but the survey-measured cognitive anxiety is not there. The study was small, and it is the one that put a number on it.
